text: Becca, it would be interesting to test the cameras specifically for real-world sharpness, shutter behavior, and how well each one preserves fine detail in normal everyday use. That matters a lot to me, because on paper newer phones often look better, but in practice they do not always produce the sharpest photos. For example, I still find that my Pixel 3 XL can deliver very crisp and detailed images. The Pixel 3 XL used a 12.2 MP main camera with 1.4 μm pixels and Google’s HDR+ pipeline with zero-shutter-lag multi-frame capture, which helped it preserve detail very well in many casual shooting situations. Newer Pixel models use much larger main sensors and different processing priorities, which improve light capture and low-light capability, but they can also change the rendering style and motion handling. In some situations, especially when light is lower or subjects move, that can translate into softer-looking images or less natural fine detail. Google has also explained that low-light denoising and multi-frame capture can require more or longer frames, which increases the risk of blur when either the subject or the phone moves. So while newer Pixels are often better at brightness, dynamic range, and night performance, I do not always find them better at producing the sharp, highly detailed look I used to get from the Pixel 3 XL.

video_title: It’s time for a change... (1,000 photos with the S26 Ultra)
text: So I sort of agree & disagree with this take all at the same time. I actually think the stagnation of Samsung photos is a positive, they've become so uniform and locked in that you know what they're good and bad for. I still see people complaining about shutter lag & other things but it all feels tech envy related to me - if you want to buy the latest & greatest wild Chinese phone, fine. What I do know is they had focus issues with the S20 Ultra but since the 21 (which I owned) up through now with the 26, there's no real problems with shooting these cameras & I'm able to get all different kinds of shots with easy corrections *because* I know what each lens is good for & how their processing pipeline holds up. Where I *do* think they're falling behind is that there's been no real reason to swap between these devices in the previous 5 years because they've all functionally done the same thing within an acceptable range. If you're nearer the start of that cycle (say S20 - S22/23) I'd say there's no real reason to get an S26 & you're better waiting. But equally, whenever Samsung do change their tech, they usually have some kind of hardware issues & you're better waiting a generation for the fix. So you can take a chance next year with the 27 and hope they've added in MagSafe and new lenses across the board, but you're more likely to get something with focusing issues than if you wait another year for the S28. I just hope behind the scenes they're doing all that QA now rather than just accepting people will keep buying phones even when they launch with issues. But to be clear, as with big full frame cameras, you don't need the latest & greatest all the time with these devices. They're adding at most 1 - 2% most years and (worryingly) actually getting slightly worse and removing things like remote shutter or the periscope zoom in this newest phone. TL;DR the best camera is the one you know reliably, and wait for a solid big generational leap before you upgrade so they can work out all the gremlins.

text: I don't think that prolonging the battery lifetime is the concern when they can outright say battery needs additional care with lowering voltage to drastically lower the charge speed and SOT. As a pixel 4a and 7 user I've done extensive tests after the battery limiting update and thanks to higher ambient temp 35-45C I can give some pointers. I've always documented the battery charger counter using aida64 charging to 100% after unboxing it. In my case 4a had rated capacity of 3400mAH as opposed to nominal capacity of 3080mAh ± 200mAh whereas Pixel 7 has 4700mAh against nominal capacity of 4300mAh. Both were bought after an year of their USA release in India. Depending on the extent you discharge the battery < 10% you'll usually lose 50mAh upon the full charge to 100% i.e Amp reading on Aida64 will be <10mA to indicate full charge which usually happens 30 mins even after showing the battery is full. If you add high ambient temperatures and heavy CPU/GPU/TPU load into the mix you'll lose 150-250mAh. Repeat this process until you hit the BHA algorithm's milestone (s) that will compensate by using advanced wear leveling calculation and find the best max voltage the battery can currently do is 4.25V instead of the rated 4.45V which might not seem that big but reduces the max capacity you can charge and discharge by another 200mAh on top of early wear level. Lithium ion battery perform at their peak with 4.3-4.5V and <3.7 V is termed as dead. Currently on the 4a the battery won't charge if you have drained the battery from 100-20% twice in a day and percentage will be stuck until you reboot or do battery reset by holding power button for 10 seconds to initiate it. Currently typing from pixel 4a with current voltage at 3.74V and on my pixel 7 it's at 4.3V from the earlier 4.45V with charge cycle of 652 (after 3 years of use). I do use xtar power bank (molicell,lg and sony battery cells) that can revive dead li-ion and regulate high wear level batteries to function properly. Also the side effect is the phone gets warm quickly even on idle or screen turned off on some days. Been waiting to swap the 7 with the 10 on launch but I don't want to deal with early battery swap or any software remedies even with TSMC SoC. Then again Pixel 4a and others can be switched to graphene OS or flashed to older OS which doesn't have rollback protection to alleviate the battery health maximising algorithm.

text: Imagine you have a picture on your computer. When you "digitally zoom" in, you're just enlarging the pixels in that picture. The image gets bigger, but it also gets blurry and you lose quality, just like when you zoom in on a photo you've already taken on your phone. Optical zoom is completely different. Think of it like a pair of binoculars. When you use binoculars, they have a special lens that physically brings the far-away object closer to your eyes before the image is even captured. So, when a phone like the Pixel 10 has a dedicated 5x optical zoom camera, it's like a built-in pair of binoculars. It has a separate lens specifically for that 5x zoom, so it's a completely new, high-quality photo taken at that distance. It's not just a digital crop of the main camera, which is what most phones do when you zoom past their optical limit. That's why the quality is so much better and clearer—it's using real lenses to get closer, not just software.

When compared to an older model, the Pixel 10 might lag slightly in night photography. Furthermore, the Pixel 10 features significant upgrades in other areas. It includes a 10.8MP telephoto camera with 5x optical zoom, a better processor compared to the previous model, faster charging, and a larger battery capacity. Moreover, when compared to a device like the Xiaomi 14T PRO (I had been using xiaomi phones since Xiaomi 12), the overall user experience regarding software, photos, and AI capabilities is significantly different. These differences are substantial enough to make choosing the Google Pixel 10 phone the clear decision. On the negative side, I would add the limited storage capacities available (128/256 GB) and its high price.

Ultimately it made me realise that as much as I looooove modern Android compared to iOS, I really don't need to switch from iOS right now even though I'm nowhere near deep in the Apple ecosystem as much as others are. The money spent on the phone combined with the small things I'm losing (like location tracking with my family or opening links in specific apps, which somehow iOS does better than Android nowadays) and the fact that my current phone is really completely fine unfortunately made me decide to return it. A bunch of the things you mentioned in the review don't apply to me either and while it looks to be perfect for someone more active and out and about like that, it was one more confirmation for me that returning it was the right decision. That being said, it was definitely fun to mess about with and helped improve my life on the other side so I'm rather thankful for it funnily enough. text: The funny thing to me is how many people will always say polished metal is slippery just because it looks shiny. Scientifically, it's literally the opposite. When it comes down to it, polished metal is completely flat, meaning way more of your skin is actually making direct contact with it to create friction. Something like brushed aluminum has all these microscopic peaks and valleys, so your hand is only touching the very tops of the metal. Plus, your fingers naturally have a little bit of moisture and oil on them. When you hold a perfectly smooth surface, it creates a microscopic suction effect called capillary adhesion. With a matte or brushed finish, air gets into all those tiny grooves and completely ruins that grip. I don't understand why people see a mirror finish and automatically think it's like ice, but the physics just doesn't back it up at all.

text: To be honest, this time I really respect Vivo and OnePlus smartphones — their pricing feels much more justified. You’re getting everything you need without overpaying, unlike what people do for the Pixel 10 Pro and other so-called Pixel series phones. In the past, I used to dislike iPhones, but I have to admit: when you pay for an iPhone, yes, the brand value is high — but you also get excellent video quality, top-notch microphones, outstanding speakers, and a smooth software experience. (The Theories) Users and reviewers have a few theories, none of them confirmed by Google: Software Legacy: Google's entire portrait algorithm was built around using dual-pixel data from a single wide-angle sensor (back from the Pixel 2). Users speculate that Google has simply refused to or has been too lazy to re-engineer its entire portrait pipeline to incorporate data from two separate lenses (the main + telephoto) for depth mapping. Hardware Quality: This is a strong theory for the base model Pixel 10. As we discussed, the telephoto lens on the base 10 is a smaller, lower-quality 10.8MP sensor. It's possible this sensor doesn't perform well in anything but perfect lighting, so Google forces the camera to use the superior (but downgraded) 48MP main sensor for all portrait processing, as it can gather more light and detail. Pro Model Differentiation (Which Failed): The baffling part is that even the Pixel 10 Pro (with its high-quality 48MP telephoto) also doesn't use the 5x lens for portrait mode, which debunks the "Pro" differentiation theory and points back to a core software/philosophy problem. The "Workaround" (And Why It's Not Good Enough) Users have found a workaround, but it's clunky and highlights the problem: Switch to the regular "Photo" mode. Manually select the 5x telephoto lens. Take a regular, non-portrait photo. Go into Google Photos, find the picture, tap "Edit," and use the "Portrait blur" tool to artificially add the blur after the fact. While the server-side AI for this tool is very good, users are annoyed that this is an extra, multi-step process instead of a simple, real-time feature in the main camera app.

text: Google’s Tensor AI chip is the smartest move they’ve made since launching Pixel. For this kind of price tag, the box should come with at least the basics or even a nice case or accessory to reward loyal Pixel owners. Google has fired a bullet at Apple with Tensor, but by copying Apple’s worst habit selling less in the box for more money they risk souring the very audience that’s cheering them on. Brilliant strategy, disappointing execution at the checkout.

text: A battery cycle on an iPhone is 100% of total charge used, not one trip from 0 to 100. Apple literally defines it this way. If you charge 80 → 100%, you’ve added 20% of a cycle. If later you charge 50 → 70%, that’s another 20%. Eventually all these little chunks add up to 100%, and then it counts as one cycle. So yes — partial charges absolutely contribute to the cycle count. It’s like filling a bucket: ten small 10% pours still fill it. A useful comparison: Think of cycle count like kilometres on a car. You don’t have to drive a full tank from empty to full; every little trip adds to the odometer. If you want your battery to last longer, the healthiest range tends to be 20%–80%, but modern iPhones are pretty smart, so don’t stress each charge.

text: I just went from an iPhone 14 Pro Max to an iPhone 17 base, and the only “complaint” I have is screen size. I lost a little bit of screen size, but for my stubby fingers, it’s actually become a blessing in disguise. The little bit small size means I can do more, on my phone, with only one hand. I have significant carpal tunnel in both hand, and reaching with my dominant thumb was starting to becoming painful from over stretching. With the slightly smaller screen, i don’t have to stretch as much. When I first went to look at upgrading, I wrote down a list of important things that I need vs. want, and the base iPhone 17 met all those features. If I want a bigger screen, I can mirror to my TV or get out my iPad. If I need more advanced photo editing, I can easily switch to my Mac Mini. I didn’t need all the bells and whistles that I needed when I chose the iPhone 14 Pro Max. I’m a few days into this new phone, and I haven’t found a feature on the base model that I miss that was exclusive to the Pro models. Maybe my 14 Pro Max was outdated enough to make me think that the 17 is amazing, but so far, I got a phone at half the price and I’m missing nothing!

text: 13 Pro Max users READ THIS I used the iphone 17 for around 24 hours and the phone is good phone do not get me wrong however coming from a 13 pro max these are the things i will say: Size: coming from the 13 pro max the size of the of the iphone 17 is noticeable but not that different. I will say if you have been using a smaller phone since forever then by all means this iphone is the best ever for you hands down. If you are a Pro Max user like myself you will definitely get jealous of a 17 Pro Max user once you hold their phone in your hand (this is from experience please trust me). Weight: I can tell you for a fact it was such a shock to hold this phone i will not lie to you it is so light compared to a 13 pro max like unimaginable and so unreal its crazy that a phone so light could be so powerful. Having felt the weight of the iphone 17 max as a 13 pro max user i will say it is much more comfortable to use and is lighter to use which is insane. The way i hold my iphone 13 pro max is i have my pinky at the bottom the phone, the finger close to my pinky and middle finger stretched at the edge and then the finger close to my thumb centered around the middle and then i use my thumb to type and its so much easier to do this on 17 pro max Battery: I have not used an iphone 17 pro max to test battery however from the people i know who has the 17 pro max they say the battery is the best ever and coming from a Pro Max line up i feel you will get extra confidence knowing that your phone is now set for the future in the long run and the upgrade will feel more worth it. Like i said i am speaking to 13 pro max users however the battery on the 17 was just as impressive i will say. Display: This is bright as hell dude like when i compared it to my 13 pro max it was absolutely noticeable and i love it. When i compared to how snappy it felt from 13 pro max you can tell the difference so i can’t even imagine how nice it is on the 17 pro max. If you are a small phone user you will not be disappointed with the display. Speakers: This little guy is really really loud i couldn’t begin to tell you how shocked i was when this thing played music it was sick deffo an upgrade. Dynamic Island: Coming from a 13 pro max we don’t get this luxury and for a few extra bucks i would say its worth having compared to what we get on the 13 pro max. Camera control & Action Button: i personally like these new features so getting this on either phone is just a plus dude especially coming from a phone that doesn’t have them. Selfie Camera and Camera: Wow lets just say game changer from 13 pro max its astounding definitely an upgrade which either one you go for Future Planning: i feel like the 12gb gives me a safer or confidence booster that if i don’t upgrade in the next year or 2 years that the phone will be equipped for any future software upgrade or AI upgrades so thats something u will need to take into consideration however if you are a casual user it won’t matter. All in all if you are 13 Pro Max user please do not make the mistake of going for the base 17. Yes you get a ton of upgrades but you will miss that screen and i feel like you just get added bonuses which is a bigger screen, better battery with a brand chip to help with performance, comfort and much better cameras which is why i am returning it. SMALL PHONE USERS - Best ever phone you can get a hold of right now.

text: This is an outstanding and, above all, realistic 10-hour battery drain test! It’s impressive to see the Samsung S26 Ultra staying within a tiny 3-minute margin of the iPhone 17 Pro Max, despite stuck with the proven 5,000 mAh capacity. Let’s be real: calling a 3-minute difference a 'lag' ignores the actual user experience. Much more exciting is the boot speed: seeing the direct comparison, the iPhone feels like a snail starting up compared to the S26 Ultra. That’s the true power of the Snapdragon 8 Elite and the optimized UFS storage. However, what’s missing in this test (and almost all others) is a re-test after 14 days of usage. During the first few days, the Galaxy AI works overtime in the background to analyze user behavior and index data. Only after this learning phase does 'Adaptive Battery' fully kick in to proactively manage background drain. I’d bet that in a two-week re-test, that 3-minute gap doesn't just disappear – the S26 Ultra likely pulls ahead of the iPhone thanks to this intelligent background hygiene. I’m also quite critical of the comparison with the Honor Magic 8 Pro. Sure, 6,270 mAh sounds great on a spec sheet, but what about software sovereignty in 5 years?. Who guarantees that Honor users will still get Android updates in 2031 or won’t be forced into a different OS due to sanctions?. Samsung guarantees 7 years of updates and monthly security patches. To me, true sustainability means a device physically designed for cell protection (60W instead of 100W+ stress) and a software fortress that stays secure until 2033. text: You're mixing up some stuff here. SoC (state of charge) is not the same as SoH (state of health). But you're right: Google's BHA system strives to slow battery aging, keep SoH high for longer. It does this by reducing top voltage (the very most at 100% SoC) ever so slightly and reducing charging Amperage to adapt to higher temperatures caused by battery degradation. Not every phone does this in a controlled way like BHA. It usually happens AFTER the cell has already aged and degraded. It's basically like fighting the cause of aging (BHA) vs fighting the symptoms. Also a phone slowing down due to aging is NOT due to the battery not being able to supply enough votage - CPU voltage is not directly related to battery voltage, it gets converted first. What happens with age is called thermal throtteling, which occurs due to excess heat buildup from rising internal resistance. What you refer to is a system in old iPhones where they limited performance proactively. Your conclusion is totally correct though! It's a pro-consumer feature that got poorly communicated.
